chief_complaint: neck stiffness and pain after rear-end car crash
hpi_details: 30-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of severe posterior neck pain and stiffness that began the morning after a rear-end motor vehicle collision. She was wearing a seatbelt and did not strike her head. Denies numbness, tingling, or weakness in her arms.
ideas: She thinks the jolt from the collision jarred the joints in her neck loose or caused a hairline fracture.
concerns: She is worried that she will not be able to turn her head to drive safely and will have to miss several shifts at her new job.
expectations: She hopes to get an X-ray to confirm no bones are broken, a supportive foam neck collar, and a doctor's note excusing her from work for a few days.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Cervical whiplash is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Cervical Whiplash: Gentle range of motion, avoid hard collar, NSAIDs, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Cervical whiplash.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Cervical fracture (must be excluded by imaging criteria) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Any midline bony tenderness, neurological deficit, or high-risk mechanism would need imaging per Canadian C-spine rules.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 30F presenting with acute posterior neck pain and stiffness 24 hours after a low-speed rear-end motor vehicle accident. No radicular symptoms.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Severe diffuse tenderness to palpation over the cervical paraspinal muscles and trapezius. No midline bony tenderness over the spinous processes. Neurological exam of bilateral upper extremities is fully intact. Normal reflexes.
reference_soap.plan: Perform and document a focused neurologic examination and apply the Canadian C-spine Rule. If there are no high-risk features, no midline tenderness, and the patient can actively rotate the neck 45 degrees in both directions, imaging is generally not indicated. Encourage early gentle range of motion; consider a short course of analgesia, including an NSAID only if safe for the patient's risk profile. Avoid routine cervical collars and urgently reassess any neurologic deficit or evolving red flag.

red_flags: Any midline bony tenderness, neurological deficit, or high-risk mechanism would need imaging per Canadian C-spine rules

must_ask.say: Can you describe the accident — how fast were the cars going, and were you wearing a seatbelt?
Do you have any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your arms?

must_ask.objective: Ask about headache or dizziness (concussion screen)
must_ask.say: Did you hit your head, or have you had headaches or dizziness since?
How much can you turn your head side to side?
We recommend gentle range-of-motion exercises rather than a rigid collar, along with anti-inflammatory medication.

history.answer: My neck has been really stiff and painful since this morning after I was rear-ended in a car crash yesterday.
The collision happened yesterday afternoon, but I felt mostly okay until I woke up this morning with terrible stiffness and aching.
I was stopped at a red light when another car hit me from behind at low speed. I had my seatbelt on and the airbags did not go off.
No, my head did not hit the steering wheel or headrest hard, and I never blacked out or lost consciousness.
The pain is across the back of my neck and down into both of my shoulders. It does not shoot down into my arms or hands.
It feels like a deep, severe muscle ache and intense tightness, around a seven out of ten.
My neck feels locked up, and it hurts a lot whenever I try to turn my head to the left or right.
It was really intense when I got out of bed this morning and has stayed steady throughout the day.
Turning or bending my neck in any direction makes the ache much sharper.
Resting my head back against a firm pillow eases the tension slightly, but the pain does not fully go away.
No, I do not have any numbness, tingling, or pins and needles anywhere in my shoulders, arms, or fingers.
No, my arms and hands feel just as strong as usual, and I can grip objects normally.
No, I have not had any headache, lightheadedness, or dizziness.
No, my vision is fine, and I have not had any nausea, vomiting, or trouble concentrating.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, I have had no problems controlling my bowel or bladder.
No, I have never had any neck pain, spine trouble, or prior motor vehicle accidents before this.
I tried placing a warm heating pad on my neck for twenty minutes this morning, but I have not taken any pain medications yet.
It was difficult checking my blind spots while driving, and sitting at my desk working on my computer has been miserable.
I thought the violent jolt from the car hitting me knocked something out of place in my spine or caused a small hairline fracture.
I'm worried I won't be able to drive or sit at my desk on Monday, and missing shifts at my new job will look really bad.
I'm hoping you can take an X-ray to confirm nothing is broken, give me a neck brace for support, and write a medical note for my employer.
I do not have any chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine products.
I only drink a glass or two of wine socially on weekends.
I work as an office accountant and live in an apartment with my husband.
My parents are both healthy, and there is no family history of spine or neurological disorders.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, my cycles are regular, and there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert and in mild discomfort holding her neck still, but in no acute distress.

Severe diffuse tenderness across bilateral cervical paraspinal muscles and upper trapezius without midline spinous process tenderness; active cervical rotation is limited to 45 degrees bilaterally by pain and muscle tightness.
Full 5/5 muscle strength in bilateral shoulder abduction, elbow flexion and extension, wrist extension, and finger grip.
Intact and symmetric sensation to light touch and pinprick throughout bilateral C5 through T1 dermatomes.
Biceps, brachioradialis, and triceps deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with negative Hoffmann signs.
Alert, fully oriented to person, place, and time with clear speech and intact recall.
Cranial nerves II through XII are intact with normal pupillary reflexes and full extraocular movements without nystagmus.
Gait is steady and smooth, Romberg test is negative, and finger-to-nose testing is intact bilaterally.
